raw_response:
I've been working this land in Quzhou for five decades. I know these soils, I know when the rains come and when they don't, and I know what the markets in the county want. At 70, with just my wife and me, I'm not going to chase after every new technique — but I'm educated enough to know what works and what doesn't.

**My thinking, crop by crop:**

**Cabbage (spring and autumn):** Cabbage is my bread and butter. I split it across two seasons — 1 mu in spring and 1.5 mu in autumn. Autumn cabbage always fetches better prices and stores longer. I've been using F1 hybrids for 15+ years; the heads are uniform and buyers prefer them. I'll apply rotary tillage before transplanting, as I always do, and keep up with aphid and caterpillar sprays — three rounds in spring, four in autumn when pressure is heavier.

**Maize:** Two mu of summer maize. It fits cleanly between the spring cabbage and the overwintering spinach in my rotation. I use hybrid seed —郑单958 or similar — because the yield difference is not debatable after all these years. Three irrigations from my well will cover jointing, tasseling, and grain fill. I don't need more than two pesticide passes if I scout regularly.

**Spinach:** Half a mu, overwintering. I plant this after the maize comes off. Spinach in winter sells well locally. I use an improved variety, not hybrid — the cost isn't justified for spinach. I'll keep nitrogen modest; too much and the leaves go soft and rot under frost.

**Chili:** Half a mu is enough. It's labor-intensive to pick and I'm not as fast as I was at 50. Chili needs careful irrigation — drought stress at flowering kills the yield — so six irrigations from the well. Four pesticide passes for mites and botrytis.

**Kidney bean:** Half a mu, spring. I still use seed I've saved and selected over the years. Being a legume, it fixes some nitrogen and I don't push fertilizer on it. It's low-effort and gives us fresh beans through early summer, plus some to dry and sell.
